title: Searching Filesystems & Bulk Operations (`find`, `-exec`, `-delete`, `xargs`)
why_it_matters: Production servers accumulate tens of thousands of log files, old release artifacts, and corrupted 0-byte temp files. Knowing how to locate files by name, type, age, size, or permissions using `find` and safely act on them with `-delete`, `-exec`, or `xargs` is a daily DevOps superpower.
concept_explanation:
1. `find` Evaluates Live Filesystem Metadata (Chapter 17): Unlike `locate` (which reads a prebuilt database), `find <dir>` walks the directory tree in real time and filters entries using tests:
   - Type: `-type f` (regular file), `-type d` (directory), `-type l` (symbolic link)
   - Name: `-name '*.conf'` (case-sensitive) or `-iname '*.yaml'` (case-insensitive)
   - Size: `-size +100M` (greater than 100 MB), `-size -10k` (less than 10 KB), `-empty` (0-byte file or empty directory)
   - Time: `-mtime +7` (modified more than 7 days ago), `-mmin -30` (modified within the last 30 minutes)
   - Permissions: `-perm 0600` (exact mode match)

2. Combining Tests with Logical Operators:
   - Tests listed side-by-side have an implicit `-and` (e.g., `find cluster_data -type f -empty` matches entries that are regular files AND 0 bytes).
   - Use `-or` (`-o`) for either condition, and `-not` (`!`) to negate a test.

3. Acting on Found Files (`-print`, `-delete`, `-exec`, `xargs`):
   - `-print` is the default action (prints matching paths to stdout, which you can pipe to `sort` and redirect `> file.txt` as learned on Day 1).
   - `-delete` removes matching files directly (`find cluster_data -type f -empty -delete`). Always run without `-delete` first to preview what will be removed!
   - `-exec cmd {} \;` runs `cmd` once per file, whereas `-exec cmd {} +` batches filenames into a single command invocation for speed.
   - `xargs` reads filenames from stdin and passes them as arguments to a command (`find . -type f -name '*.bak' | xargs rm -f`).
cheat_sheet: find cluster_data -type f -empty                  # Preview all 0-byte regular files inside cluster_data
find cluster_data -type f -empty -delete          # Delete all 0-byte regular files inside cluster_data
find cluster_data -type f -name '*.conf' | sort   # Find all .conf files and sort paths alphabetically
find cluster_data -type f -name '*.bak' -delete   # Delete all .bak files recursively
find . -type f -name '*.sh' -exec chmod 755 {} +  # Batch-apply chmod 755 to all .sh scripts

lab.title: Clean Up Corrupted 0-Byte Artifacts, Purge Stale `.bak` Files & Inventory `.conf` Files with `find`
lab.description: Practice using `find` tests (`-type f`, `-empty`, `-name`) and actions (`-delete`, piping to `sort`) inside `workspace/devops/day-006`:
tasks: 2. Use `find cluster_data -type f -empty -delete` to locate and delete ALL empty (0-byte) files inside `cluster_data/` while leaving non-empty files untouched.
3. Use `find` to locate and delete all files ending with `.bak` inside `cluster_data/` (`find cluster_data -type f -name '*.bak' -delete`).
4. Use `find cluster_data -type f -name '*.conf'` to list all `.conf` files inside `cluster_data/`, pipe to `sort`, and redirect stdout into `workspace/devops/day-006/conf_files.txt`.

verifications.description: All 0-byte files inside cluster_data/ have been deleted, and all 3 non-empty .conf files remain intact
All stale .bak files inside cluster_data/ have been removed
conf_files.txt lists all 3 .conf files (coredns.conf, nginx.conf, redis.conf)

quiz.question: As taught in Chapter 17 of The Linux Command Line, what is the difference between ending `find ... -exec gzip {} \;` with a semicolon (`\;`) versus ending with a plus sign (`+`)?
options: B) `\;` executes `gzip` once per matching file, whereas `+` combines all matching filenames into a single `gzip` command invocation
C) `+` deletes the files without running `gzip`
quiz.explanation: Ending `-exec` with `+` appends the found paths into a single command execution (similar to `xargs`), avoiding spawning a separate process for every single file.

quiz.question: Which `find` test matches ONLY regular files (excluding directories, symlinks, and device nodes)?
quiz.explanation: In `find`, `-type f` matches regular files, `-type d` matches directories, and `-type l` matches symbolic links.

quiz.question: Which `find` expression locates regular files modified MORE than 14 days ago and larger than 100 Megabytes?
quiz.explanation: In `find`, `+N` means greater than N and `-N` means less than N. So `-mtime +14` is > 14 days old, and `-size +100M` is > 100 Megabytes.

quiz.question: Why should you always run a `find` command WITHOUT `-delete` first before re-running it with `-delete`?
options: A) `find` refuses to run `-delete` on the first execution
B) Running without `-delete` uses the default `-print` action so you can visually verify the exact list of matching files before permanently deleting them
C) `-delete` only works after caching filenames in `/tmp`
D) Running without `-delete` creates a backup automatically
quiz.explanation: As emphasized in both Chapter 17 and today's video, testing your `find` expression first prints all matches safely so a typo in `-name` doesn't wipe out unintended files.

quiz.question: Which `find` command locates all 0-byte regular files inside `/var/tmp`?
quiz.explanation: Combining `-type f` (regular files) with `-empty` (0 bytes) finds all empty files inside `/var/tmp`.
